problem_solving_method: Split grading into a pure, Flask-free rules engine (grading.py) that evaluates one subject at a time and returns the mark, grade point, and which published rule (R-10/R-11/R-12/R-13/R-29) decided it, so the trace the office sees is generated from the same code path that produced the GPA, not written separately. Marks for 60 students are generated once at start-up (data.py): 8 students are hand-built to hit every edge case named in the problem statement, the remaining 52 are randomised on a fixed seed for reproducibility. app.py evaluates all 60 once at start-up and serves three read-only views: the class ledger, a per-student trace, and the office checking list.

R1.evidence: data.py: build_roster_and_students() — 60 students across Class 9A / Class 9B, 6 compulsory subjects + 1 optional per student, 2 subjects (Science, ICT) carry separate theory/practical marks. 8 explicit edge-case students in _edge_case_students(): compulsory fail with strong average (9A-01), practical fail with passing theory (9A-02), optional subject below the point where it helps (9A-03), absence in a compulsory subject (9A-04), plus 4 additional edge cases (optional-only absence, practical-only absence, a perfect A+, and an exact letter-grade boundary).

R2.evidence: grading.py: evaluate_subject() and evaluate_student() — grade point per subject, GPA via the R-13 formula, letter grade via R-10. Rendered per student at the /student/<id> route (app.py) and templates/student.html.

R3.evidence: templates/student.html — every subject shows the real mark(s) used, the grade point produced, and the deciding rule (R-11/R-12/Grading scale). When a compulsory failure cancels the result, the uncancelled average is shown alongside the published 0.00/F so the failing subject and the missed average are both visible (see student 9A-01).

R4.evidence: /checklist route (app.py) and templates/checklists.html — three R-29 lists (optional-subject, practical-fail, absent) each with a per-student reason string, built directly from the same evaluate_student() output used for the GPA.

team_members.major_contribution: Made the grading engine, Flask routes, templates, and synthetic student dataset, including the 4 required edge-case students. Designed the CSV upload format and validation, and wrote the README and evaluation-manifest.json.

major_design_decisions: Kept all graded results and raw marks in server-side in-memory dicts (RESULTS, RAW_MARKS) rather than a database, since the roster is small, judging is a single-session activity, and it keeps the whole system inspectable as three plain Python modules with no migrations or ORM.

Derived the CSV upload format (required columns, per-column value ranges) programmatically from the live subject roster instead of hardcoding it, so the upload page's documented format and the parser's validation can never fall out of sync if the roster changes.

AB (absent) is only ever accepted as the literal text 'AB' — an empty cell is always rejected rather than silently treated as an absence — to stop a blank spreadsheet cell from accidentally failing a student.

Every SubjectResult carries the rule code (e.g. R-11, R-12, R-13) and a plain-language note explaining exactly why a mark produced the grade it did, so the individual marksheet doubles as an audit trail rather than just a final number.

GPA is rounded with Decimal + ROUND_HALF_UP to 2dp rather than Python's built-in round(), so boundary GPAs (e.g. exactly 3.50) land on the correct letter grade deterministically rather than depending on binary float rounding.

The 'uncancelled average' required by R-13 is computed for every student, not only failing ones, so the same code path produces both the published GPA and the audit figure — there is no separate 'what if' calculation that could drift out of sync.

Absence in only the practical half of a practical subject (theory present, practical blank) is treated as an absence for the whole subject, since R-12 does not split theory/practical explicitly. This is flagged as an interpretive call, not a certainty, in known_limitations below.
All 60 students are evaluated once at process start-up and held in memory, since this is a read-only judging/demo tool rather than a live data-entry system; there is no need to recompute per request.
known_limitations: Absence in only the practical part of a practical subject (see major_design_decisions) is an interpretive reading of R-12, not an explicitly confirmed one — worth a judge's ruling if it matters to scoring.
No persistence layer or database; marks live in data.py and are regenerated identically on every restart from a fixed seed. There is no teacher-facing form to enter or correct marks.
No authentication on /upload or /student/<id>/edit — anyone with the URL can add or change marks; acceptable for a single-judge/single-session demo but not production-ready.

CSV parsing expects a well-formed header row with the exact expected column names (case/space/hyphen-insensitive); it doesn't attempt to auto-detect delimiters or alternate encodings beyond UTF-8/UTF-8-BOM.
app.secret_key is a hardcoded development placeholder, used only to enable flash messages — not suitable for a real deployment.
